traits.smithy.api#documentation:
Amazon EventBridge Custom Event Bus

Amazon EventBridge event bus API. An event bus receives events published by your applications and AWS services, stores them for a configurable retention period, and delivers them to subscribers. A subscriber filters events, optionally transforms them, and invokes a target such as Lambda, SQS, SNS, Kinesis, Step Functions, or an HTTP endpoint. The API manages event buses, subscribers, event sources, resource policies, and tags, and publishes events through PutEvents and PutRawEvents.

UseDualStack.documentation: When true, use the dual-stack endpoint.

UseFIPS.documentation: When true, send this request to the FIPS-compliant regional endpoint.

The maximum number of events to include in a single batch delivered to the target. The service delivers up to this many events per batch; fewer may be delivered when the batch window elapses or the target's per-batch limit is smaller. This is a maximum, not a guaranteed count. Valid range is 1-500 (default: 10, or the target API's per-batch maximum). The resolved value applied by the service is returned on read.

The maximum time in seconds to wait for a batch to fill before delivering it to the target. This is a maximum; a batch may be delivered sooner if it reaches MaxBatchSize or another delivery condition is met. Valid range is 0-300 (default: 0, meaning no wait). Lifecycle state of an event bus.

  • CREATING: Bus creation is in progress.

  • CREATE_FAILED: Bus creation failed; see StateReason. The bus cannot be recovered or recreated in place: delete it with DeleteEventBus, then create a new bus.

  • ACTIVE: Bus is fully operational and can accept events.

  • UPDATING: Bus update is in progress.

  • UPDATE_FAILED: Bus update failed; the bus remains operational with its previous configuration.

  • DELETING: Bus deletion is actively in progress.

  • DELETE_FAILED: Bus deletion failed; see StateReason. Retry DeleteEventBus after removing subscribers and event sources.

A client-supplied precondition (e.g. ExpectedRevisionId on a resource-policy write) did not match the current state of the resource. Retrying the same request will fail again; re-read the resource and re-evaluate before retrying.

A conditional request is not retry-safe on its own. If an earlier attempt committed but its response never reached the caller, retrying fails with this error, which is indistinguishable from another writer having won. Compare the resource's current contents with what the request intended: a successful attempt stores a revision ID the caller never saw, so the revision alone cannot tell the two apart, but matching contents mean the change took effect.

The ARN of the destination that receives events that could not be delivered. An Amazon SQS queue is the supported destination. The queue-name grammar mirrors SQS's own rule: 1-80 chars of [A-Za-z0-9_-], where a FIFO name's ".fifo" suffix counts toward the 80 (so a FIFO base name is at most 75 chars). Deletes the named resource policy attached to an event bus.

The delete succeeds only if the named policy's current revision ID matches this value; if it differs or the policy does not exist, the operation fails with ConflictException. The "NO_POLICY" sentinel is not valid here. When omitted, deleting an absent policy is an idempotent success. Supplying this value makes the delete non-idempotent: once it succeeds the expected revision no longer exists, so retrying an unanswered request fails with ConflictException even though the policy was deleted. To establish the outcome, read the policy back: ResourceNotFoundException means the delete took effect.

Which named policy to delete. Defaults to "default" when omitted (a delete AWS Resource Access Manager makes on the owner's behalf resolves to "AWS_RAM" instead). The two writers are exclusive in both directions — only Resource Access Manager can delete "AWS_RAM", and only the bus owner can delete "default" — so naming the other party's policy fails with AccessDeniedException. A well-formed name that is neither of the two fails with InvalidInputException.
The Amazon Resource Name (ARN) that uniquely identifies an event bus.
Revision ID of the policy that was deleted. Absent when no policy was deleted.

EventBusActive.documentation: Waits until the event bus reports ACTIVE. Use after CreateEventBus (bus starts in CREATING) or UpdateEventBus (bus moves to UPDATING) before invoking operations that require an ACTIVE bus. Fails fast on the terminal failure states CREATE_FAILED, UPDATE_FAILED, and DELETE_FAILED, surfacing StateReason. CREATING, UPDATING, and DELETING are intentionally unmodeled intermediate states that fall through to the implicit retry.

EventBusDeleted.documentation: Waits until the event bus is fully deleted, signaled by DescribeEventBus returning ResourceNotFoundException. Use after DeleteEventBus. Fails fast on the terminal DELETE_FAILED state, surfacing StateReason; retry DeleteEventBus after removing subscribers.

MskSubscriberActive.documentation: Waits until an Amazon MSK subscriber's connectivity reports ACTIVE. Use after CreateSubscriber or UpdateSubscriber on a subscriber that targets an MSK cluster. Fails fast on PROVISION_FAILED, surfacing MskDetails.StateReason. PROVISIONING falls through to the implicit retry. Applies only to MSK subscribers; other subscribers return no MskDetails, so the waiter times out.

Attaches a named resource policy to an event bus — the only resource type that supports policies; other resource ARNs are rejected. Each bus holds two named policies: "default" (customer-managed, full IAM policy language including Deny) and "AWS_RAM" (written exclusively by AWS Resource Access Manager to reflect resource shares). Both policies are evaluated on cross-account authorization; an explicit Deny in either overrides an Allow in the other. Operations that omit PolicyName target "default". A "default" policy that would grant public access is rejected with PublicPolicyException and is not attached; this check is always on and cannot be disabled.

The write succeeds only if the named policy's current revision ID matches this value; a policy that does not exist yet matches only the sentinel "NO_POLICY" (create-only). On mismatch the operation fails with ConflictException. When omitted, the write is unconditional. Every attempt stores a newly generated revision ID, so retrying an unanswered request can conflict with the caller's own earlier attempt; read the policy back and compare it with the one you intended before treating a conflict as another writer's change.

A well-formed name that is neither of the two fails with InvalidInputException.

Sets a new credential on a webhook EventSource. If you supply Credential, EventBridge uses that value. Otherwise, EventBridge generates one. For HTTP Basic authentication, only the password changes. The username does not change. EventBridge never returns the credential. To read a generated value, call secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret that SecretArn identifies.

You can rotate the credential of an EventSource in the ACTIVE, UPDATING, or UPDATE_FAILED state. For a revoked EventSource or an EventSource in any other state, EventBridge returns InvalidStateException. EventBridge also returns InvalidStateException if the secret of the EventSource is scheduled for deletion or has been deleted.

If you rotate the credential of one EventSource too many times in 24 hours, EventBridge returns LimitExceededException. Retry later. The limit becomes available again automatically.

If AWS Secrets Manager throttles the call, EventBridge returns ThrottlingException. Retry later.

To use this operation, you must have the following permissions in your IAM policy:

  • secretsmanager:PutSecretValue on the secret of the EventSource

  • secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret of the EventSource, for HTTP Basic authentication only

  • kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt on the AWS KMS key that encrypts the secret

The resource policy of the secret must not deny the secretsmanager actions.

EventBridge accepts the new credential when this call returns. In rare cases, the new credential takes up to 2 minutes to reach every EventBridge endpoint.

EventBridge also accepts the previous credential for 15 minutes after the rotation. The window ends at the CreatedDate of the AWSCURRENT secret version plus 15 minutes. Only the credential that the most recent rotation replaced stays valid. If you rotate again within 15 minutes, the older credential stops working immediately.

A retry with the same ClientToken within 8 hours returns the same result and does not rotate again. A retry of a rotation that supplied a value can arrive after a later rotation completed. In that case, the retried value becomes the current credential, and the credential it replaces does not stay valid.

Name of an event bus. The first character must be alphanumeric; the remaining characters may also include '.', '-', and '_'. The grammar matches the name segment of EventBusArn (event-busv2/<name>/<id>), so every valid name can be represented in the bus's ARN. The same type is used everywhere a bus name appears.

Lifecycle state of an event bus.

  • CREATING: Bus creation is in progress.

  • CREATE_FAILED: Bus creation failed; see StateReason. The bus cannot be recovered or recreated in place: delete it with DeleteEventBus, then create a new bus.

  • ACTIVE: Bus is fully operational and can accept events.

  • UPDATING: Bus update is in progress.

  • UPDATE_FAILED: Bus update failed; the bus remains operational with its previous configuration.

  • DELETING: Bus deletion is actively in progress.

  • DELETE_FAILED: Bus deletion failed; see StateReason. Retry DeleteEventBus after removing subscribers and event sources.

Human-readable explanation of why an event bus is in its current State. Omitted when the bus is in a normal operational state (ACTIVE). It stands in for the error response an asynchronous failure cannot return, so it applies only to resources with an asynchronous lifecycle: event buses. EventSources and subscribers are provisioned synchronously and report failures directly on the request.

The name of the header that carries the message ID. Required when SignedMessageComposition is MESSAGE_ID_DOT_TIMESTAMP_DOT_BODY. Requests whose message ID contains a period (.) are rejected. Reserved names are rejected, as described on StaticTokenAuthConfiguration's TokenHttpHeader.

How the secret is encoded. RAW uses the secret's characters as the signing key. BASE64 decodes the secret first, as providers that follow the Standard Webhooks specification require. The default is RAW.

The signing key shared with the provider. If you omit it, EventBridge generates one. EventBridge stores the key only in AWS Secrets Manager and never returns it, including from DescribeEventSource. The key must be 16 to 512 bytes; with BASE64 SecretEncoding, this is measured after decoding.

The name of the header that carries the signature, for example X-Hub-Signature-256. When TimestampHttpHeader names the same header, Delimiter, SignaturePrefix and TimestampPrefix are all required. Reserved names are rejected, as described on StaticTokenAuthConfiguration's TokenHttpHeader.
The text that precedes the signature in the header value, for example sha256=. Required when TimestampHttpHeader is the same header as SignatureHttpHeader.

How the provider assembles the message it signs from the request.

  • BODY - The request body alone. BODY provides no replay protection.

  • TIMESTAMP_DOT_BODY - <timestamp>.<body>. Requires TimestampHttpHeader.

  • MESSAGE_ID_DOT_TIMESTAMP_DOT_BODY - <messageId>.<timestamp>.<body>, as in the Standard Webhooks specification. Requires TimestampHttpHeader and MessageIdHttpHeader.

The name of the header that carries the request timestamp. Required when SignedMessageComposition is TIMESTAMP_DOT_BODY or MESSAGE_ID_DOT_TIMESTAMP_DOT_BODY, or when TimestampToleranceInSeconds is set. Not allowed when SignedMessageComposition is BODY, because BODY does not sign the timestamp. Reserved names are rejected, as described on StaticTokenAuthConfiguration's TokenHttpHeader.
The text that precedes the timestamp in the header value, for example t=. Required when TimestampHttpHeader is the same header as SignatureHttpHeader.

The maximum difference, in seconds, allowed between the request timestamp and the time EventBridge receives the request. Requests outside this window are rejected. The default is 300 seconds. Requires TimestampHttpHeader. Not allowed when SignedMessageComposition is BODY, because BODY does not sign the timestamp.

The token the provider sends in the header. If you omit it, EventBridge generates one. EventBridge stores the token only in AWS Secrets Manager and never returns it, including from DescribeEventSource. EventBridge compares it against the entire header value, so a provider that sends Authorization: Bearer <token> needs SecretValue to include the "Bearer " prefix.

The name of the header that carries the secret, for example X-Webhook-Secret. Reserved names are rejected: the names EventBridge's edge writes, such as Host and the X-Forwarded-* family, and the hop-by-hop and framing names an HTTP intermediary may rewrite, such as Connection and Content-Length. Authorization is allowed.
